gloss: A feature so typical of someone or something that it identifies them.
examples: Attention to detail is the *hallmark* of her work.
Cheap tickets and long lines are *hallmarks* of the festival.
Careful planning is a *hallmark* of good management.

gloss: A drug that makes people see or hear things that are not there.
examples: LSD is a powerful *hallucinogen*.
The study looked at how *hallucinogens* affect the brain.
Certain mushrooms contain a natural *hallucinogen*.

gloss: Any of the chemical elements chlorine, fluorine, bromine, iodine, and astatine.
examples: Chlorine and iodine are *halogens*.
A *halogen* bulb gets much hotter than an LED.
Fluorine is the most reactive *halogen*.

gloss: A very small village.
examples: They live in a *hamlet* of about forty people.
The road winds through several *hamlets*.
The chapel is the only public building in the *hamlet*.
contrast: Capitalized, *Hamlet* is Shakespeare's play; the ordinary noun means a tiny village.

gloss: A team sport in which players throw a ball into the other team's goal with their hands.
examples: She played *handball* in college.
We used to play *handball* against the school wall.
*Handball* is far more popular in Europe than in the United States.

gloss: A short book of instructions or facts about a subject.
examples: Check the employee *handbook* for the vacation policy.
The store sells repair *handbooks* for most cars.
Every new student gets a *handbook* on the first day.

gloss: One of a pair of metal rings joined by a chain, locked around a prisoner's wrists.
examples: The officer put *handcuffs* on him.
One *handcuff* was still attached to the rail.
He was led out of the courthouse in *handcuffs*.
contrast: Nearly always plural: *handcuffs*.

gloss: Something that makes progress harder, or an advantage given in sport to a weaker player.
examples: His golf *handicap* is down to eight.
Not speaking the language was a real *handicap*.
The race gives *handicaps* to the fastest horses.
contrast: Used of people, *handicap* is dated and often offensive; say *disability*.

gloss: A skill of making things by hand, or an object made that way.
examples: The market sells local *handicrafts*.
She teaches a *handicraft* class at the community center.
Weaving is a traditional *handicraft* in this valley.

gloss: The way something is touched, moved, or dealt with.
examples: Shipping and *handling* is another twelve dollars.
The box is marked for careful *handling*.
People criticized the mayor's *handling* of the flood.

gloss: The act of passing something, such as a ball or a job, to another person.
examples: The quarterback made a quick *handoff* to the running back.
We need a clean *handoff* between the two teams.
*Handoffs* between shifts are where mistakes usually happen.

gloss: The formal transfer of power, duties, or property to someone else.
examples: The *handover* of power took place at noon.
There was no real *handover* when she left the job.
Both sides agreed on a peaceful *handover*.

gloss: A saw with a wide blade and a handle, used by hand rather than by motor.
examples: Cut the board with a *handsaw* if you don't have a power saw.
His grandfather's *handsaw* still hangs in the shop.
Two *handsaws* were missing from the toolbox.

gloss: The part of a telephone that you hold to your ear and mouth.
examples: Put the *handset* back on the cradle.
The hotel phone has a heavy *handset*.
New *handsets* are shipping next month.

gloss: The act of balancing upside down on your hands with your feet in the air.
examples: She can do a *handstand* against the wall.
The kids were doing *handstands* in the pool.
Hold the *handstand* for ten seconds.

gloss: A person paid to do small repairs around a house or building.
examples: We hired a *handyman* to fix the porch.
Good *handymen* are booked weeks out.
My uncle works as a *handyman* in the neighborhood.
contrast: Irregular plural: *handymen*.

gloss: A man whose job was to execute prisoners by hanging.
examples: The *hangman* was waiting at the top of the steps.
In those days the county paid a *hangman*.
The novel opens with a *hangman* checking his rope.
contrast: *Hangman* is also a word-guessing game; the plural is *hangmen*.

gloss: A small torn piece of skin at the edge of a fingernail.
examples: I have a *hangnail* that keeps catching on everything.
Don't bite your *hangnails*.
A *hangnail* can get infected if you pull at it.

gloss: A strong wish for something, often something simple.
examples: I've got a *hankering* for barbecue.
She had a *hankering* to see the ocean again.
Every fall he gets a *hankering* to go hunting.

gloss: A sign that something is coming.
examples: Robins are a *harbinger* of spring.
The quiet report was a *harbinger* of the layoffs to come.
Falling orders are often *harbingers* of a slowdown.

gloss: Tough, aggressive behavior used to win, especially in business or politics.
examples: The union is playing *hardball* in the talks.
This is *hardball* politics, not a debate club.
He plays *hardball* whenever money is on the line.

gloss: Someone who refuses to soften a strict political position.
examples: *Hardliners* in the party blocked the deal.
He is a *hardliner* on immigration.
The new leader is widely seen as a *hardliner*.

gloss: How firm a material is, or how much mineral a water supply contains.
examples: The lab measured the *hardness* of the steel.
Water *hardness* varies a lot across the county.
Diamond sits at the top of the *hardness* scale.

gloss: Difficult conditions of life, especially from a lack of money.
examples: Many families are facing real financial *hardship*.
The fund helps students who can document *hardship*.
He grew up in *hardship* and never complained about it.

gloss: The women of a Muslim household of the past, or the rooms they lived in.
examples: The palace tour includes the *harem*.
The sultan's *harem* occupied a whole wing.
A bull elephant seal guards a *harem* of females.

gloss: A musician who plays the harp.
examples: A *harpist* played during the ceremony.
She is the orchestra's principal *harpist*.
The planner booked two *harpists* for the reception.

gloss: An early keyboard instrument whose strings are plucked rather than struck.
examples: Bach wrote a great deal of music for the *harpsichord*.
The museum keeps two restored *harpsichords*.
A *harpsichord* cannot play loudly and softly the way a piano can.

gloss: The quality of being severe, rough, or unkind.
examples: The *harshness* of his tone surprised everyone.
People complained about the *harshness* of the sentence.
Winter here is known for its *harshness*.

gloss: A dish of chopped cooked meat and potatoes fried together.
examples: He ordered corned beef *hash* and two eggs.
I made *hash* out of last night's roast.
The diner's *hash* comes with toast on the side.

gloss: A drug made from the resin of the cannabis plant.
examples: Customs officers found *hashish* in the spare tire.
*Hashish* is stronger than the dried leaf.
He was arrested for selling *hashish*.

gloss: Something annoying that takes more trouble than it should.
examples: Parking downtown is such a *hassle*.
Renewing the permit turned into a real *hassle*.
The new system took a lot of *hassles* out of billing.

gloss: Speed in doing something, especially when it causes mistakes.
examples: In his *haste* he left his wallet on the counter.
*Haste* makes waste.
The report was written in *haste* and it shows.

gloss: A small door in a floor, ceiling, ship, or aircraft.
examples: The crew climbed down through the *hatch*.
Close the *hatch* before we take off.
Both cargo *hatches* were sealed for the crossing.

gloss: A very strong feeling of dislike toward someone or something.
examples: The comment section was full of *hate*.
*Hate* has no place in this community.
He was charged with a *hate* crime.

gloss: Someone who criticizes or attacks another person out of dislike or envy.
examples: Don't let the *haters* get to you.
Every popular show has its *haters*.
He's a *hater* of anything new.

gloss: The hip and upper thigh of a person or animal.
examples: The dog sat back on its *haunches*.
He crouched on his *haunches* by the fire.
The butcher cut a *haunch* of venison.

gloss: A safe place where someone or something is protected.
examples: The island is a *haven* for migrating birds.
The country became a tax *haven*.
The shelter offers a safe *haven* for families.

gloss: Great damage or confusion.
examples: The storm wreaked *havoc* along the coast.
The strike played *havoc* with our schedule.
One bad line of code caused *havoc* on the site.

gloss: A thorny shrub or small tree with white flowers and red berries.
examples: A *hawthorn* grows at the corner of the field.
The *hawthorns* are covered in white blossom in May.
Birds strip the *hawthorn* of its berries by December.

gloss: A small tree or shrub that produces hazelnuts.
examples: A row of *hazels* screens the garden from the road.
The nuts come from a *hazel*, not from a walnut tree.
He cut a walking stick from a young *hazel*.
contrast: *Hazel* is also an eye color: *hazel eyes* are greenish brown.

gloss: Dangerous chemical or biological material that needs special handling.
examples: A *hazmat* team closed the highway for six hours.
The workers wore *hazmat* suits and masks.
The spill was treated as a *hazmat* emergency.

gloss: A decorated covering worn on the head, often for a ceremony.
examples: The dancers wore feathered *headdresses*.
Her *headdress* was made of silk and glass beads.
The museum displays a ceremonial *headdress*.

gloss: Anything worn on the head, especially for protection.
examples: Wrestlers are required to wear *headgear*.
The shop sells helmets and other protective *headgear*.
Mandatory *headgear* cut the number of head injuries.

gloss: A hold in which you grip someone's head under your arm.
examples: His brother put him in a *headlock*.
The wrestler broke out of the *headlock*.
The boys rolled around the lawn trading *headlocks*.

gloss: A man in charge of a school, especially a private one.
examples: The *headmaster* called my parents.
She was named *headmaster* of the academy last spring.
Two former *headmasters* came to the reunion.
contrast: American public schools have a *principal*; *headmaster* is used mainly at private schools.

gloss: The space above a person's head, or spare room in a budget or limit.
examples: There isn't much *headroom* in the back seat.
Watch your head — the basement has low *headroom*.
The budget leaves a little *headroom* for repairs.

gloss: A square of cloth tied over the hair.
examples: She tied a *headscarf* over her hair before going out.
Bright *headscarves* hung across the market stall.
A *headscarf* is required inside the mosque.
contrast: The plural changes f to v: *headscarves*.

gloss: A photograph of a person's face and shoulders, used professionally.
examples: Every actor needs a good *headshot*.
Send us a *headshot* and a short bio.
The firm updated all the *headshots* on its website.

gloss: The act of balancing upside down on your head and forearms.
examples: He can hold a *headstand* for a full minute.
We worked on *headstands* in yoga class.
A *headstand* takes more balance than strength.

gloss: Forward progress toward a goal.
examples: We finally made some *headway* on the project.
The talks made little *headway* this week.
The boat made slow *headway* against the current.

gloss: A wind blowing straight against the direction you are moving.
examples: A strong *headwind* added an hour to the flight.
The riders fought a *headwind* the whole way home.
The company is facing economic *headwinds*.

gloss: The process of becoming healthy or whole again.
examples: The cut is slow in *healing*.
*Healing* takes longer at his age.
The town needs time for *healing* after the shooting.

gloss: One movement of the heart as it pumps blood, or the rhythm of those movements.
examples: The doctor listened for a *heartbeat*.
Her *heartbeat* slowed as she calmed down.
I'd move back in a *heartbeat*.

gloss: Someone who makes people fall in love and then leaves them, or a painfully close loss.
examples: The game was a real *heartbreaker* — they lost by one point.
He was a *heartbreaker* back in high school.
Last-second losses like that are *heartbreakers*.

gloss: A burning feeling in the chest caused by acid from the stomach.
examples: Spicy food gives me *heartburn*.
She takes something for *heartburn* after dinner.
*Heartburn* has nothing to do with the heart.

gloss: The central region of a country, seen as the home of its traditional life.
examples: The candidate campaigned across the American *heartland*.
Corn from the *heartland* feeds much of the country.
Factory towns in the industrial *heartlands* have struggled.

gloss: A good-looking famous man that many people are in love with.
examples: He was the *heartthrob* of every teen magazine.
The show's *heartthrob* got the loudest cheers.
Old *heartthrobs* still turn up on nostalgia tours.

gloss: A low evergreen plant with small purple or white flowers that grows on open land.
examples: The hills were purple with *heather*.
*Heather* grows well in poor, acid soil.
She pressed a sprig of *heather* in her book.

gloss: The system that keeps a building warm, or the warmth it provides.
examples: The *heating* went out during the cold snap.
*Heating* costs jumped this winter.
The house has radiant floor *heating*.

gloss: A boxer in the heaviest weight class, or an important and powerful person.
examples: He fought as a *heavyweight* for ten years.
Two industry *heavyweights* backed the plan.
The *heavyweight* title fight sold out in a day.

gloss: The belief or habit that pleasure is the most important thing in life.
examples: The novel is a study in *hedonism*.
He defended a life of quiet *hedonism*.
Critics dismissed the show as pure *hedonism*.

gloss: A person who lives for pleasure.
examples: He calls himself an unapologetic *hedonist*.
The resort is built for *hedonists*.
A *hedonist* would say that pleasure is the whole point.

gloss: Control or dominating influence by one country or group over others.
examples: The book traces the rise of American *hegemony*.
Smaller cities resisted Athenian *hegemony*.
Their *hegemony* over the market lasted a decade.

gloss: A woman who will inherit or has inherited great wealth.
examples: She's the *heiress* to a hotel fortune.
Two *heiresses* contested the will.
The *heiress* gave most of the money away.
contrast: The h is silent — it sounds like AIR-uhs, the same start as *heir*.

gloss: A valued object passed down in a family for generations.
examples: The watch is a family *heirloom*.
She grows *heirloom* tomatoes every summer.
The fire destroyed dozens of *heirlooms*.
contrast: The h is silent: the word begins like *air*.

gloss: A robbery, especially a large and carefully planned one.
examples: The movie is about a diamond *heist*.
Police are calling it the biggest *heist* in the city's history.
A string of bank *heists* hit the area last year.

gloss: A place where helicopters take off and land.
examples: The hospital has a *heliport* on the roof.
A new *heliport* opened near the river.
Both *heliports* were closed by fog.

gloss: The wheel or handle that steers a ship, or the position of leader.
examples: The captain took the *helm* himself.
She has been at the *helm* of the company for six years.
He stepped down and left the *helm* to his deputy.

gloss: The feeling or state of being unable to do anything about a situation.
examples: There was a real sense of *helplessness* after the flood.
*Helplessness* is common in the first weeks of caregiving.
He described a feeling of complete *helplessness*.

gloss: A poisonous wild plant, or the deadly drink made from it.
examples: Socrates was sentenced to death and made to drink *hemlock*.
*Hemlock* grows in the ditch along the back road.
Cattle have died from eating *hemlock*.
contrast: In the U.S. *hemlock* is also a common evergreen tree, which is not poisonous.

gloss: The red substance in blood that carries oxygen around the body.
examples: Her *hemoglobin* was low, so the doctor prescribed iron.
*Hemoglobin* carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues.
The test measures *hemoglobin* levels.
contrast: American spelling; the British write *haemoglobin*.

gloss: An inherited disease in which the blood does not clot properly.
examples: *Hemophilia* runs in his mother's family.
Treatment for *hemophilia* has improved enormously.
He was born with a severe form of *hemophilia*.
contrast: American spelling; the British write *haemophilia*.

gloss: A swollen vein around the anus that can bleed and hurt.
examples: The doctor said the bleeding was from *hemorrhoids*.
Sitting all day can make a *hemorrhoid* worse.
There are creams for *hemorrhoids* at any drugstore.
contrast: Usually used in the plural; the British spell it *haemorrhoid*.

gloss: A reddish-brown dye made from a plant, used on hair and skin.
examples: She dyes her hair with *henna*.
The bride's hands were painted with *henna*.
*Henna* fades from the skin after a couple of weeks.

gloss: A sign of something to come, or in the past an official messenger.
examples: The first robins are a *herald* of spring.
In the play a *herald* announces the king's arrival.
Falling prices were the *herald* of a bad year for farmers.

gloss: Someone who treats illness with medicines made from plants.
examples: She sees an *herbalist* for her allergies.
The *herbalist* mixed a tea of dried roots and bark.
*Herbalists* have used this plant for centuries.
contrast: In American English the h is silent — UR-buh-list; the British say HUR-buh-list.

gloss: The passing of physical qualities from parents to children.
examples: Height is largely a matter of *heredity*.
The class covered genes and *heredity*.
Both *heredity* and diet play a role in the disease.

gloss: A belief that goes against the official teaching of a religion or group.
examples: The council condemned two *heresies* that year.
Questioning the coach's system is a kind of *heresy* around here.
Medieval *heresies* often began as reform movements.

gloss: Someone who holds a belief that a religion or group rejects.
examples: He was tried as a *heretic*.
*Heretics* were driven out of the city.
In this office she's a *heretic* for preferring paper files.

gloss: A person who lives alone and away from other people.
examples: He lives like a *hermit* up in the hills.
The cave was home to a *hermit* for twenty years.
Medieval *hermits* often settled near a busy road.

gloss: A condition in which an organ pushes through a weak spot in the muscle around it.
examples: He's having surgery for a *hernia* next month.
Lifting that box the wrong way could give you a *hernia*.
Two kinds of *hernias* are common in men.

gloss: Very brave behavior in the face of danger.
examples: The firefighters were honored for their *heroism*.
The book is full of quiet, everyday *heroism*.
It took real *heroism* to go back inside.

gloss: A person who is sexually attracted to people of the opposite sex.
examples: The survey included both *heterosexuals* and gay respondents.
He identifies as a *heterosexual*.
The law applies equally to *heterosexuals* and same-sex couples.

gloss: A rough rule that gives a good enough answer quickly.
examples: "Buy the cheaper one" is a useful *heuristic*.
The program uses a simple *heuristic* to rank results.
People rely on mental *heuristics* to make fast decisions.

gloss: A small charcoal grill of Japanese design, or the flat grill used in a Japanese restaurant.
examples: We grilled shrimp on the *hibachi*.
The restaurant has *hibachi* tables where the chef cooks in front of you.
He bought a little *hibachi* for the balcony.

gloss: A tropical plant with very large, brightly colored flowers.
examples: A red *hibiscus* was blooming beside the door.
*Hibiscus* tea is served cold here.
She planted three *hibiscuses* along the fence.

gloss: A sudden sharp sound made in the throat, or a small unexpected problem.
examples: I've had the *hiccups* all morning.
There was a small *hiccup* in the schedule.
Hold your breath and the *hiccups* usually stop.
contrast: Also spelled *hiccough*, but said the same way: HIK-uhp.

gloss: A red mark on the skin left by kissing or sucking.
examples: He tried to hide a *hickey* under his collar.
She came home with a *hickey* on her neck.
*Hickeys* fade after a few days.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A North American tree with hard wood and edible nuts, or the wood itself.
examples: The old *hickory* by the barn came down in the storm.
The axe handle is made of *hickory*.
*Hickory* smoke gives the ribs their flavor.

gloss: A quiet private place where someone goes to be away from others.
examples: They rented a little *hideaway* in the mountains.
The bar is a *hideaway* for locals who want quiet.
He has *hideaways* all over the state.

gloss: A secret place where someone hides, especially from the police.
examples: Police found the gang's *hideout* in an empty warehouse.
The cabin served as a *hideout* for months.
They moved between three different *hideouts*.

gloss: A picture used as a written character in ancient Egyptian writing.
examples: The walls are covered in *hieroglyphs*.
Each *hieroglyph* can stand for a sound or a whole idea.
Scholars finally learned to read the *hieroglyphs* in the 1820s.

gloss: The best or most memorable part of something.
examples: The trip to the coast was the *highlight* of our vacation.
The news showed *highlights* from the game.
Her speech was the *highlight* of the evening.

gloss: A head covering worn in public by some Muslim women.
examples: She wears a *hijab* to work.
The shop sells scarves and *hijabs*.
He asked whether the *hijab* was required in the building.

gloss: Loud laughter and amusement.
examples: His answer caused general *hilarity*.
The video was met with *hilarity* online.
There was a lot of *hilarity* at the rehearsal dinner.

gloss: A country person from a remote hill area — usually an insult.
examples: The show played every *hillbilly* stereotype it could find.
He jokes that he's just a *hillbilly* from the hollow.
City reporters wrote condescending stories about the *hillbillies*.

gloss: The highest part of a hill.
examples: The church sits on a *hilltop* above the town.
We watched the sunset from the *hilltop*.
White houses dot the *hilltops* along the coast.

gloss: The handle of a sword or knife.
examples: His hand rested on the *hilt* of his sword.
The blade went in up to the *hilt*.
The museum's swords have beautifully decorated *hilts*.

gloss: Something that makes an action slower or harder.
examples: The new rules are more of a *hindrance* than a help.
Bad weather was the biggest *hindrance* to the search.
Small *hindrances* added up to a long delay.

gloss: Understanding of an event that you only have after it has happened.
examples: In *hindsight*, we should have left an hour earlier.
*Hindsight* makes everything look obvious.
With the benefit of *hindsight*, the deal was a mistake.

gloss: An indirect suggestion, a small piece of advice, or a very small amount.
examples: Give me a *hint* — I'm completely stuck.
There was a *hint* of lemon in the sauce.
The article has *hints* for first-time buyers.

gloss: A young person of the 1960s and 1970s who rejected ordinary society, or anyone with that style today.
examples: His parents were *hippies* in the seventies.
She looks like an old *hippie* in that vest.
The town still has a *hippie* feel to it.
contrast: Also spelled *hippy*.

gloss: A very large African animal with thick gray skin that lives in rivers.
examples: The zoo's *hippo* has a new calf.
*Hippos* spend most of the day in the water.
A *hippo* can outrun a person on land.
contrast: Short for *hippopotamus*.

gloss: A person who has just been given a job.
examples: She's our newest *hire*.
The company made twelve *hires* last quarter.
He turned out to be a very good *hire*.
contrast: In American English a *hire* is usually the person hired, not the act of hiring.

gloss: A chart of bars showing how often values fall into each range.
examples: The *histogram* shows how the test scores were spread out.
Draw a *histogram* of the results.
Both *histograms* have roughly the same shape.

gloss: An expert in history, or someone who writes about it.
examples: The *historian* spent ten years in the archives.
*Historians* still argue about the causes of the war.
She's a *historian* of the American South.

gloss: A small problem that delays something, or the bar for towing a trailer.
examples: The ceremony went off without a *hitch*.
There was one small *hitch* with the paperwork.
The trailer connects to a *hitch* on the back of the truck.

gloss: In baseball, the player whose turn it is to bat.
examples: He's the best *hitter* on the team.
The pitcher struck out three *hitters* in a row.
She's a power *hitter* who can clear the fence.

gloss: A store of valuable or useful things that someone has collected and hidden.
examples: A farmer found a *hoard* of Roman coins in his field.
He kept a *hoard* of candy under the bed.
Several Viking *hoards* are on display in the museum.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *horde* (a large crowd).

gloss: Someone who collects and keeps far more things than they can use.
examples: My aunt is a *hoarder* — she can't throw anything away.
The show follows *hoarders* as they clear out their homes.
He became a *hoarder* after his wife died.

gloss: An activity you do regularly for pleasure in your free time.
examples: Photography started as a *hobby* and became a job.
He has too many *hobbies* and not enough time.
Do you have a *hobby* outside of work?

gloss: Someone who does an activity as a hobby rather than for a living.
examples: The kit is aimed at *hobbyists*, not professionals.
He's a serious model-train *hobbyist*.
Most of the club members are weekend *hobbyists*.
